claims.text: Nanoparticles with minimal atomic mismatch will retain a single-phase solid solution throughout 473–1923 K.
For low-mismatch nanoparticles, configurational entropy offsets the relatively low strain energy and preserves the solid solution.
Nanoparticles with higher atomic mismatch accumulate enough strain energy to overcome entropic stabilization during high-temperature exposure.
High atomic mismatch leads to phase segregation or chemical ordering at high temperatures.
The comparison begins with nanoparticles containing at least five metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and crystallized as homogeneous single-phase solid solutions.
Minimal- and high-mismatch nanoparticle sets will be subjected to identical thermal treatments over 473–1923 K.
An inert atmosphere avoids oxidation during the thermal treatment.
Atomic mismatch is reflected in differences in atomic radii, cohesive energies, and surface energies.
The degree of atomic mismatch determines intrinsic strain within the nanoparticles.
In high-mismatch nanoparticles, increased strain energy triggers thermally activated diffusion.
Thermally activated diffusion facilitates phase segregation or chemical ordering during high-temperature exposure.
Low-mismatch nanoparticles will remain structurally and compositionally homogeneous relative to their as-synthesized baseline.
High-mismatch nanoparticles will develop new diffraction peaks, compositional gradients, or secondary phases at higher temperatures.
New diffraction peaks, compositional gradients, or secondary phases indicate segregation or ordering.
Differences in atmosphere, heating or cooling rates, and dwell times could obscure the effect of atomic mismatch on stability.

Equivalent single-phase stability in both mismatch groups, or segregation in the low-mismatch group while the high-mismatch group remains homogeneous, would falsify the proposed mismatch-governed stability relationship.
